title: Supercooled Pig Kidneys Transplanted Successfully After 72 Hours in 'Landmark' Study
summary: Time is the enemy of organ donation. Once removed, a kidney starts deteriorating, and surgeons have roughly 24 hours to transplant it. But what if that window could stretch to days? In a groundbreaking study, researchers at Texas A&M University supercooled pig kidneys to -4°C—below the freezing point—and stored them for up to 72 hours before successful transplantation. The key is a hermetically sealed chamber that maintains constant pressure, preventing ice from forming without the need for cryoprotectants, which can have side effects. 'I always describe this as low-tech high science,' said Matthew Powell-Palm, the thermodynamicist leading the work. The organs were submerged in a standard preservation solution. After 24, 48, or 72 hours of supercooling, each kidney was transplanted back into the original donor pig, whose other kidney was removed. The 24-hour supercooled kidneys began producing urine immediately and reached normal function within about 10 days—faster than kidneys kept on ice for 24 hours. Even after 72 hours, recovery outpaced the clinical gold standard. Over 30 days, the pigs grew by 30%, and the kidneys nearly doubled in size to compensate. One pig was monitored for 200 days, and its kidney remained healthy. Kevin Myer, CEO of LifeGift, called it 'a landmark achievement.' With over 104,000 Americans waiting for a kidney and 17 dying daily, the shortage is dire. Many donated kidneys are discarded because they degrade before reaching a recipient. This device could revolutionize organ preservation, buying precious time for matching and transport. While earlier studies used cryoprotectants, this pressure-based method avoids them, potentially simplifying regulatory approval. The team is 'really, really pumped' and aims to bring this technology to human transplants, offering new hope to thousands.
why_it_matters: This breakthrough could drastically reduce the number of kidneys that go to waste, saving thousands of lives each year. It also opens the door to building organ banks, where organs could be stored for days or weeks, transforming transplant medicine from a frantic race against time to a carefully planned procedure.

background_read: Kidney transplants are life-saving procedures, but a severe shortage of donor organs means many patients wait years for a match.
Currently, donated kidneys are kept on ice at near-freezing temperatures and must be transplanted within about 24 hours before damage sets in.
This time limit contributes to the discard of roughly one in five donated kidneys each year, even though they could have helped someone.
The new technique builds on decades of cryobiology research, which explores how to preserve living tissue at extremely low temperatures without ice crystals forming and shredding cells.

Researchers at Texas A&M University, led by thermodynamicist Matthew Powell-Palm, designed a device that uses pressure, not chemicals, to keep organs in a supercooled state, following earlier experiments that used cryoprotectants with mixed results.
Kevin Myer, CEO of LifeGift—a non-profit that coordinates organ donation—praised the work as a 'landmark achievement'.

perspectives.description: Patients would no longer have to gamble on a last-minute match; stored organs could be delivered across the country, increasing fairness. The extended window means more donated kidneys can find a suitable recipient, reducing deaths on the waiting list.

The technology is still experimental and studied only in pigs; it may face unforeseen biological hurdles when applied to humans. Rushing into costly trials without long-term safety data could lead to complications like delayed organ rejection or hidden cell damage.

Pressure-based supercooling avoids the toxicity of chemical cryoprotectants, but the exact mechanisms by which it prevents ice formation at the cellular level need deeper study. Understanding this could reveal fundamental principles of how water behaves in living tissues under extreme conditions.

If success continues in human trials, this device could become standard equipment in hospitals, and the same principle might be adapted for livers, hearts, and other organs. That would fundamentally reshape organ transplantation logistics and could one day allow true organ storage banks.
